verses.bibleText:
Masters, give unto
your servants that which is just and equal; knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter begins by completing the household instruction that started in Colossians 3:18. Enslaved persons had been told to serve sincerely because Christ was their true Lord and because every wrong would come under impartial judgment. Masters now hear the corresponding command. Their social position gives them no exemption from accountability, and their authority cannot be exercised according to whim, economic advantage, or personal anger.

In the Roman world, an enslaved person was legally treated as property, and the master possessed extensive power over work, movement, punishment, and family life. Against that background, the requirement to provide what is “just and equal” carries considerable moral force. Paul addresses masters as people responsible before God for the welfare of those placed under their authority. Enslaved persons are not invisible tools of production; they are fellow human beings whose treatment must be governed by justice. Colossians 3:11 has already declared that within the new humanity there is neither bond nor free as a basis for spiritual worth, for Christ is all and in all.

The command does not present the institution of slavery as God’s ideal. Rather, the lordship of Christ enters an existing and deeply unjust social order and begins to overturn its assumptions. The master is reminded that he too is under authority. The same word can describe both the earthly master and the heavenly Lord, but the contrast is decisive: the earthly master possesses limited, temporary authority; Christ possesses absolute authority and judges without partiality. No social rank, wealth, or legal privilege will shield an oppressor in the judgment.

“Knowing that ye also have a Master in heaven” transforms authority into stewardship. Those who employ, supervise, teach, govern, or lead must treat others as persons for whom Christ cares. Earthly power is never ownership of another person’s dignity. The greater one’s authority, the more searching one’s accountability before the Lord who sees concealed exploitation as clearly as public conduct. Justice toward others does not earn salvation, but it reveals whether the professed servant of Christ has truly submitted to the righteous Master in heaven.

wordNotes.term: just and equal — δίκαιον καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα (dikaion kai tēn isotēta)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression joins what is morally right with what is equitable or fair. Isotēs can denote equality, but in this setting it emphasizes impartial and just treatment rather than arbitrary rule. Masters must give enslaved persons what accords with God’s righteous standard.

verses.bibleText: Continue in prayer, and watch in the same with thanksgiving;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From the ordering of the household, the letter turns to the praying life of the whole congregation. The command is plural: steadfast prayer belongs not merely to apostles or recognized leaders but to the entire church. The Colossians are to make prayer a continuing practice rather than an occasional response to crisis. Perseverance is necessary because answers may appear delayed, circumstances may remain difficult, and spiritual weariness may tempt believers to cease praying.

Watchfulness describes the manner in which such prayer is offered. It is the opposite of spiritual drowsiness. A watchful believer pays attention to the movements of the heart, the needs of the church, opportunities for witness, and dangers that could weaken faith. The word often appears in passages concerning the return of Christ. Such alertness is not anxious date-setting or constant searching for sensational signs. It is faithful service in the confidence that the absent Master will return. Those who watch are found praying, working, resisting evil, and caring for others when He appears.

Thanksgiving keeps watchful prayer from becoming fearful or self-absorbed. Gratitude has sounded repeatedly through Colossians because believers have been delivered from the power of darkness, forgiven in Christ, and made partakers of the inheritance of the saints. They therefore pray from within grace, not as people trying to persuade an unwilling God to become merciful. Even petitions arising from pain can be offered with remembrance of His past faithfulness.

Prayer, watchfulness, and thanksgiving belong together. Prayer without watchfulness may become mechanical; watchfulness without prayer may become anxious vigilance; petition without thanksgiving may become preoccupation with what is lacking. United, they form a life that is dependent upon God, awake to the present hour, and anchored in what He has already accomplished through Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes persistent devotion to an activity. The emphasis is not merely on emotional intensity during a single prayer but on steadfastly maintaining prayer as a settled practice of the Christian life.

Literally meaning to remain awake, the word calls for spiritual alertness. Prayer is to be offered with an awakened awareness of temptation, present responsibilities, the needs of others, and the approaching return of Christ.

verses.bibleText: Withal praying also for us, that God would open unto us a door of utterance, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in bonds:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Persevering prayer widens into intercession for the gospel mission. Paul includes himself and his fellow workers among those who need the prayers of ordinary believers. Apostolic calling does not remove dependence upon God or upon the praying fellowship of the church. The Colossians become active partners in the mission when they bring its messengers and opportunities before the Lord.

The requested opening is “a door of utterance,” more literally a door for the word. Paul’s first concern is not personal freedom, comfort, or reputation. He desires that the gospel itself be given entrance. Elsewhere an open door signifies a God-provided opportunity for proclamation, sometimes accompanied by significant opposition. An open door therefore need not mean an easy path. God may create a hearing in a prison, before hostile officials, within a household, or amid circumstances that appear to have closed every human avenue.

The message to be spoken is “the mystery of Christ.” In Colossians, mystery language confronts claims that spiritual fullness belongs to those who possess hidden teachings, ascetic techniques, or visionary experiences. God’s mystery is no longer concealed. It has been made known in Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found. Christ Himself is the center of the divine purpose: through His death comes reconciliation, through His resurrection comes new life, and through union with Him believing Jews and Gentiles belong to one redeemed people.

Paul’s chains reveal the costly setting of this request. He is bound because his proclamation of Christ has brought opposition, yet he does not regard imprisonment as proof that the mission has failed. Human beings may restrain the messenger without binding the word of God. His circumstances even become another place in which Christ may be announced.

The prayer teaches the church to seek more than the removal of obstacles. Believers may rightly pray for deliverance, but the greater request is that God will turn every circumstance into an opening for His word. Mission begins with divine initiative: God prepares occasions, awakens hearers, gives courage, and makes the message fruitful. The church participates by praying and by being ready to enter the doors He opens.

wordNotes.term: a door of utterance — θύραν τοῦ λόγου (thyran tou logou)
wordNotes.explanation: Literally, this is a “door for the word.” The image refers to an opportunity through which the gospel may advance and gain a hearing. The emphasis rests on God opening access for His message rather than merely improving the messenger’s circumstances.

wordNotes.term: the mystery of Christ — τὸ μυστήριον τοῦ Χριστοῦ (to mystērion tou Christou)
wordNotes.explanation: The mystery is God’s saving purpose, once hidden but now disclosed in and through Christ. It includes Christ dwelling among His people and the full inclusion of believing Gentiles. It is revealed gospel truth, not secret knowledge reserved for a spiritual elite.

verses.bibleText: That I may make it manifest, as I ought to speak.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The requested open door has a definite purpose: the mystery must be brought clearly into the open. God has revealed His saving purpose in Christ, and Paul is responsible to announce that revelation faithfully. The verse completes the prayer request of verse 3. Opportunity alone is insufficient if the message is confused, concealed, or shaped to avoid offence.

“To make it manifest” carries more than the idea of polished speech. Paul wants Christ to be disclosed through his proclamation. The messenger must not become the center, and the gospel must not be buried beneath speculation, verbal display, or fear of human reaction. Clarity serves revelation by allowing hearers to face the claims of Christ Himself.

“As I ought to speak” reflects a divine necessity. Paul knows himself to be entrusted with a commission, especially to proclaim Christ among the Gentiles. The word “ought” therefore expresses more than personal preference. He stands under the command of the Lord who called him. His chains have changed his circumstances but have not cancelled his calling.

The request also reveals humility. An experienced apostle still seeks prayer that he may speak as he should. Knowledge, experience, and office never make dependence upon God unnecessary. Faithful proclamation requires courage, wisdom, clarity, and sensitivity to the hearers, all without altering the truth. Weakness can become the setting in which the sufficiency of Christ is most plainly displayed. Paul asks not to appear impressive in his imprisonment, but to make the mystery of Christ unmistakable.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to reveal, disclose, or bring into the open. Paul desires to set forth plainly the mystery that God has already revealed in Christ, so that the message is neither hidden by obscurity nor distorted by fear.

verses.bibleText: Walk in wisdom toward them that are without, redeeming the time.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The movement now passes from the apostle’s witness to the congregation’s witness. Paul has asked for an open door through which the word may advance; the Colossians must live so that their daily relationships do not close doors before the gospel is heard. Mission belongs not only to public preachers. The whole church bears witness through its manner of life.

To “walk in wisdom” is to conduct oneself according to the practical understanding of God’s will. Earlier Paul prayed that the believers would be filled with spiritual wisdom so that they might walk worthy of the Lord. Here that worthy walk is viewed specifically in relation to outsiders. Christian wisdom is neither secret knowledge nor intellectual superiority. It is truth embodied in choices, habits, relationships, work, generosity, restraint, and integrity.

“Those without” are people outside the believing community. The expression recognizes a real boundary between faith and unbelief, yet the command forbids a closed or contemptuous posture. The Colossians must resist teaching that diminishes Christ while remaining lovingly engaged with neighbors who do not know Him. Separation from sin is not withdrawal from people. Christ’s people live publicly, and outsiders may judge the gospel initially by what they see in those who profess it.

“Redeeming the time” pictures the careful use of limited opportunity. The word translated “time” may point to a fitting occasion rather than merely the passing of hours. Encounters that appear ordinary can become openings for kindness, truth, reconciliation, or testimony. Such opportunities cannot always be recovered once neglected.

The urgency has an eschatological horizon. Believers live after Christ’s resurrection and before His appearing in glory. They do not know how long a particular relationship, freedom, or opening will remain. This urgency produces neither manipulation nor restless activity. It produces attentiveness. Wise witness respects the other person, refuses needless offence, and acts consistently with the gospel. A careless life can contradict even accurate words; a wise life gives those words moral credibility and may awaken a desire to know the Lord whom the believer serves.

wordNotes.term: them that are without — τοὺς ἔξω (tous exō)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase refers to people outside the Christian community. It marks a social distinction without authorizing contempt or withdrawal. The surrounding context calls believers to engage outsiders through wise conduct and gracious speech.

wordNotes.term: redeeming the time — ἐξαγοραζόμενοι τὸν καιρόν (exagorazomenoi ton kairon)
wordNotes.explanation: The idiom means buying up or making full use of the available opportunity. Kairos can denote a fitting or decisive occasion. Believers are to recognize and use God-given moments for faithful conduct and witness.

verses.bibleText:
Let your speech
be alway with grace, seasoned with salt, that ye may know how ye ought to answer every man.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Wise conduct must be matched by wise speech. The believer’s words are part of the public witness described in verse 5, whether the conversation is an explicit explanation of the gospel or an ordinary exchange in the household, marketplace, workplace, or neighborhood. The word “always” extends the command beyond special religious occasions. Grace should characterize the Christian voice as a settled quality.

Speech “with grace” is more than polished courtesy. It arises from having received God’s grace in Christ. Harshness, ridicule, dishonesty, needless argument, and contempt contradict the message of reconciliation even when the speaker’s doctrinal statements are correct. Graciousness does not mean withholding unwelcome truth or flattering the hearer. Jesus spoke words of grace while also calling people to repentance. Grace governs the motive, manner, timing, and purpose with which truth is spoken.

“Seasoned with salt” adds vividness to the instruction. Salt gave flavor and usefulness to food and was associated in various settings with preservation and wisdom. The precise shade of the metaphor need not be reduced to one meaning. Paul’s concern is clear from the result: believers should speak in a way that enables them to answer each person appropriately. Christian speech must have substance without becoming stale, warmth without becoming shallow, and conviction without becoming abusive.

The closing phrase assumes that questions will arise. A life of visible allegiance to Christ may produce curiosity, disagreement, or opposition. The believer should therefore understand the faith well enough to respond, yet the answer must be adapted to “every man.” People are not identical problems requiring a memorized formula. One may need patient explanation, another a gentle correction, another a testimony of hope, and another a respectful silence until a more suitable occasion.

The manner of answering is itself part of the answer. Words about a gracious Saviour lose credibility when delivered with pride or hostility. Conversely, pleasant speech without truth offers no saving direction. The union of grace and salt preserves both kindness and seriousness. Such speech seeks neither victory for the ego nor approval at the cost of faithfulness; it seeks to remove unnecessary barriers so that the hearer may see Christ more clearly.

wordNotes.explanation: The phrase can describe speech that is gracious in manner and speech shaped by the grace of God. In context, both ideas belong together: those who have received grace should speak in a way that communicates its character.

wordNotes.term: seasoned with salt — ἅλατι ἠρτυμένος (halati ērtymenos)
wordNotes.explanation: Salt may suggest flavor, usefulness, wisdom, or preserving influence. Here the metaphor describes speech that is neither dull nor corrupt but fitting, wholesome, engaging, and suited to the person and occasion.

verses.bibleText:
All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you,
who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter now moves into personal greetings, yet the names are more than incidental details. They reveal a gospel mission carried by a community of faithful servants. Tychicus is entrusted with reporting Paul’s circumstances and almost certainly with delivering the letter itself. In the ancient world, a trusted courier could read a letter publicly, explain its setting, answer questions, and supplement the written message with firsthand information. Paul therefore establishes clearly why the Colossians should receive him with confidence.

Three descriptions present a rich portrait of Christian service. Tychicus is first a “beloved brother.” Ministry begins within the family created by Christ, not within a hierarchy of religious importance. He is loved as a person before he is commended for a task. He is also a “faithful minister,” one who has proved dependable in service. Faithfulness, rather than visibility or personal brilliance, marks his usefulness. Finally, he is a “fellowservant in the Lord.” Paul places Tychicus alongside himself beneath the authority of Christ. Apostolic responsibility does not make Paul the master of his coworkers; both are servants of the one Lord.

“In the Lord” defines the sphere and governing reality of Tychicus’s work. He does not carry out a merely private errand for Paul. His journey, message, and pastoral care belong to Christ’s mission. The titles given to him closely resemble those earlier given to Epaphras, showing that the work is shared among trusted servants rather than centered upon one celebrated personality.

Tychicus will communicate “all” concerning Paul. The apostle’s imprisonment has not severed the bonds of fellowship, and he assumes that the Colossians care about his condition. Christian communities are not isolated units; they share burdens, news, prayer, and encouragement. Much of the church’s work continues through servants like Tychicus—people willing to travel, carry responsibility, communicate accurately, and strengthen others without seeking the prominence given to the better-known figures they assist.

wordNotes.explanation: Diakonos emphasizes active service rather than status or prestige. Tychicus is dependable in carrying out work entrusted to him for Christ and the churches.

Literally a fellow slave, the title places Tychicus beside Paul under the common lordship of Christ. Their differing responsibilities do not alter the fact that both belong to and serve the same Master.

verses.bibleText: Whom I have sent unto you for the same purpose, that he might know your estate, and comfort your hearts;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Tychicus is dispatched for pastoral reasons, not merely postal ones. Information about Paul’s condition will relieve uncertainty, bind the churches more closely together, and help the Colossians understand how the gospel is advancing despite his imprisonment. The messenger himself will become part of the encouragement he carries.

The KJV reads, “that he might know your estate,” which would mean that Tychicus is also to learn about the Colossians and report back. Another well-attested reading, reflected in many translations and matching verse 7 and Ephesians 6:22, is “that ye might know our estate.” The latter probably preserves the original wording, but the pastoral movement is mutual in either case. Paul desires genuine communication rather than distant formality between himself and the congregation.

To “comfort” their hearts means to strengthen, encourage, and steady them. The Colossians face teaching that threatens to unsettle their confidence in the sufficiency of Christ. Tychicus can confirm Paul’s message, explain his circumstances, and urge them to remain established in the faith. His presence demonstrates that encouragement is often embodied. A written word may teach, but a faithful brother who knows the situation can also listen, clarify, reassure, and call the church to perseverance. Paul sends both the letter and the servant because pastoral care requires truth communicated through trustworthy relationships.

wordNotes.term: comfort your hearts — παρακαλέσῃ τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν (parakalesē tas kardias hymōn)
wordNotes.explanation: The expression includes encouragement, strengthening, and exhortation. “Heart” refers to the inner life of thought, resolve, and affection. Tychicus is to fortify the congregation, not merely soothe its emotions.

verses.bibleText:
With Onesimus, a faithful and beloved brother, who is
one
 of you. They shall make known unto you all things which
are done
 here.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Onesimus stands beside Tychicus as a trusted bearer of news. His inclusion would have carried special weight in Colossae. The letter to Philemon reveals that Onesimus had been separated from his master under troubled circumstances and had become Paul’s spiritual son through conversion. The exact events behind that separation are not fully stated, so the common description of him as a runaway should be treated cautiously. What Scripture makes unmistakable is the transformation of his relationship to Paul, Philemon, and the church.

Paul calls him “a faithful and beloved brother.” These titles are not sentimental decorations. “Faithful” affirms his present reliability, while “beloved brother” declares his standing within the family of Christ. A man known socially as an enslaved person, and perhaps remembered for past failure, is now commended in language similar to that used for respected gospel workers. Grace has not erased his personal identity, but it has given him a new defining relationship.

“One of you” brings Onesimus home without treating him as an outsider or a permanent disgrace. He belongs among the Colossian believers. His return will require the congregation to practice the truth already stated in Colossians 3:11: in the renewed humanity, the distinction between bond and free cannot determine spiritual worth, because Christ is all and in all.

Onesimus is also entrusted with responsibility. Together with Tychicus, he will report what is happening with Paul. Restoration is therefore more than tolerating a repentant person at the edge of the community. Paul receives him, loves him, trusts him, and gives him meaningful service. The gospel creates a fellowship in which past sin can be forgiven, damaged relationships can be addressed truthfully, and a transformed person need not remain imprisoned by an old reputation. The church is called to recognize what grace has made someone, not merely what failure once revealed.

wordNotes.term: one of you — ἐξ ὑμῶν (ex hymōn)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase identifies Onesimus as belonging to the Colossian community, probably by origin as well as now by Christian fellowship. Paul publicly restores him to the congregation as a trusted brother.

verses.bibleText: Aristarchus my fellowprisoner saluteth you, and Marcus, sister’s son to Barnabas, (touching whom ye received commandments: if he come unto you, receive him;)

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Two familiar coworkers appear in this greeting, each carrying a history of costly service. Aristarchus was a Macedonian believer from Thessalonica who had already shared danger with Paul during the disturbance at Ephesus and later accompanied him on the voyage toward Rome. Paul calls him “my fellowprisoner.” The expression may mean that Aristarchus was literally confined with Paul, although the circumstances are unknown. Some understand it more broadly as an honorable description of one who had accepted captivity and suffering in Christ’s service. In either case, Aristarchus is remembered for solidarity rather than self-preservation.

Mark’s presence tells another story. The KJV calls him Barnabas’s “sister’s son,” but the Greek term means cousin. Mark had accompanied Paul and Barnabas on their earlier mission, then departed from them in Pamphylia. His withdrawal later became the cause of a sharp disagreement: Barnabas wanted to take him again, while Paul refused, and the two missionaries separated.

Years later, Mark is with Paul and sends greetings as a recognized coworker. The verse does not describe the process by which trust was restored, but the reconciliation is evident. Paul has already arranged for the Colossians to receive instructions concerning Mark and commands them to welcome him should he come. The church is therefore not to treat him according to an old failure that has been addressed and overcome. Later Paul would describe Mark as profitable to him for ministry.

The instructions previously given about Mark cannot be reconstructed with certainty. They may have concerned his travel, his reception, or questions arising from his earlier history. Speculation should not obscure the clear command: “receive him.” Paul uses his authority to secure welcome rather than exclusion.

Aristarchus and Mark display two forms of gospel grace. Aristarchus remains beside Paul in suffering; Mark returns to useful service after a serious failure. The church needs steadfast companions who do not abandon those in distress, and it also needs the humility to recognize genuine growth in those who once disappointed it. Failure can have real consequences, but it need not become a permanent identity where repentance, formation, and restored faithfulness are present.

wordNotes.explanation: The term originally evokes a fellow captive taken in war. It may indicate that Aristarchus literally shared imprisonment with Paul, though some understand it as an honorific description of shared captivity in Christ’s service.
In contemporary English the Greek word means “cousin,” not nephew. Mark was the cousin of Barnabas, helping to explain Barnabas’s close concern for him during the disagreement recorded in Acts.

verses.bibleText:
And Jesus, which is called Justus, who are of the circumcision. These only
are my fellow workers unto the kingdom of God, which have been a comfort unto me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jesus called Justus completes the group of Jewish coworkers named in verses 10-11. Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Joshua and was a common Jewish name; Justus is a Latin surname meaning just or righteous. The use of both names reflects the multilingual setting in which many first-century Jews lived and worked.

The KJV wording can sound as though Aristarchus, Mark, and Justus were Paul’s only coworkers of any kind. The following verses clearly name Epaphras, Luke, and Demas among his associates. The grammar most likely means that these three were the only coworkers from “the circumcision”—that is, the only Jewish Christians in Paul’s immediate circle who were then laboring with him for the kingdom. The statement may carry a note of sadness, since Paul deeply loved his fellow Jews and longed for their salvation.

Their work concerns “the kingdom of God.” Colossians has already described believers as transferred into the kingdom of God’s beloved Son. The kingdom is therefore present wherever Christ’s saving rule is received, the gospel advances, and lives are brought under His lordship. It also awaits its complete manifestation when Christ returns, raises His people, subdues every enemy, and delivers the kingdom to the Father. Gospel workers serve a reign already inaugurated but not yet universally revealed.

These Jewish believers had become a comfort to Paul. Their service was not confined to public proclamation; they gave personal strength to an imprisoned servant of Christ. Kingdom work includes sustaining those who suffer while carrying the mission. Presence, loyalty, practical help, and companionship can be genuine forms of ministry.

The verse also quietly displays the unity produced by the gospel. Jewish and Gentile coworkers retain their histories and identities without allowing ethnicity to determine access to Christ or worth in the church. The kingdom does not erase human distinctions by pretending they never existed. It places them under the lordship of the One who reconciles His people and calls them to labor together.

wordNotes.term: of the circumcision — ἐκ περιτομῆς (ek peritomēs)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase identifies Aristarchus, Mark, and Jesus Justus as Jewish believers. In this setting it describes ethnic and covenantal background rather than a demand that Gentiles receive circumcision.
This rare word denotes consolation, relief, or encouragement. These coworkers strengthened Paul personally while also laboring with him for God’s kingdom.

verses.bibleText:
Epaphras, who is
one of you, a servant of Christ, saluteth you, always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Epaphras appears again as a servant whose physical absence from Colossae has not diminished his pastoral concern. He is “one of you,” belonging to the community and closely identified with its spiritual life. Earlier he was described as a faithful minister through whom the Colossians learned the grace of God. He had probably played a leading role in bringing the gospel to the Lycus Valley, though the precise extent of his work cannot be reconstructed with certainty.

His defining title is “a servant of Christ.” The word can mean slave and expresses complete belonging to the Lord. Epaphras’s authority does not rest upon self-promotion, mystical claims, or social position. He serves because he belongs to Jesus Christ, and that allegiance is demonstrated in costly concern for other people.

“Labouring fervently for you in prayers” portrays intercession as struggle. The verb belongs to the same family of words Paul used for his own strenuous labor in bringing believers to maturity. Epaphras is not wrestling against God, as though divine mercy were reluctant. He is contending against discouragement, deception, temptation, and every influence threatening the congregation’s faith. Prayer is one of the principal ways in which an absent shepherd continues to serve the flock.

The purpose of his prayer is that the believers may “stand.” Stability is vital because the Colossians are being exposed to teaching that promises fullness outside the sufficiency of Christ. Epaphras asks that they remain firm, mature, and established in God’s will. “Perfect” describes wholeness or maturity, not a state in which a person has outgrown dependence upon Christ or can claim sinless self-sufficiency. Mature believers recognize their continuing need of grace while becoming less vulnerable to every persuasive error.

The KJV reads “perfect and complete,” while an ancient reading reflected in many translations has the sense “mature and fully assured.” Both direct attention toward a settled, wholehearted grasp of God’s will. Full assurance here is not careless presumption. It grows from knowing Christ, receiving the apostolic gospel, and walking obediently in what God has revealed.

Epaphras provides a model of pastoral love. He seeks neither the congregation’s admiration nor merely its outward success. He prays for people to become stable, discerning, and fully committed to God’s purposes. Some of the deepest ministry performed for another person may occur unseen, in persistent prayer before the throne of grace.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb describes striving or contending and can evoke the exertion of an athletic contest. Epaphras’s intercession is deliberate, persistent spiritual labor rather than a casual remembrance.

Here “perfect” means mature, whole, or fully developed in Christian commitment. It does not imply independent sinlessness or freedom from the continuing need of grace. The goal is stable maturity in Christ.

verses.bibleText:
For I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you, and them
that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul adds his own testimony to the description of Epaphras. The Colossians need not guess whether their absent minister still cares for them; the apostle has witnessed his zeal and labor firsthand. His concern is not expressed through occasional words of affection but through sustained exertion on their behalf.

The churches at Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis occupied the same general region of the Lycus Valley. Epaphras’s burden therefore extends beyond one congregation. He recognizes that neighboring churches share dangers, opportunities, and responsibilities. False teaching rarely respects local boundaries, and neither should faithful pastoral care become possessive or isolated.

The wording may emphasize either great zeal or costly toil. The difference does not alter the central portrait. Epaphras carries the spiritual welfare of these believers deeply enough that it costs him effort and anguish. Such burden must not be confused with anxious control. His principal action in the preceding verse is prayer, an act that entrusts the church to God rather than attempting to dominate it from a distance.

Much Christian service remains unseen by those who benefit from it. Intercession, careful thought, concern for neighboring congregations, and the emotional weight of guarding others against error may receive little public recognition. Paul deliberately bears witness to this hidden labor. The commendation encourages the Colossians to value Epaphras’s ministry and to recognize that genuine zeal seeks the maturity of the whole body rather than the reputation of the servant.

wordNotes.term: great zeal — πολὺν ζῆλον / πολὺν πόνον (polyn zēlon / polyn ponon)
wordNotes.explanation: The manuscript tradition contains readings meaning “great zeal” and “much toil” or “pain.” Both fit the context, portraying Epaphras’s intense, costly concern for the believers of the Lycus Valley.

verses.bibleText: Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas, greet you.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Two names receive a brief greeting, yet later Scripture gives them sharply different associations. Luke is called “the beloved physician.” This is the only passage that explicitly identifies his profession. He appears elsewhere as Paul’s companion, and the first-person sections of Acts strongly associate him with portions of Paul’s missionary journeys. His medical vocation may have enabled forms of practical care, but the text does not state that he served as Paul’s personal doctor. Paul’s emphasis rests on affection: Luke is beloved.

The presence of a physician among Paul’s coworkers illustrates that service to Christ does not require the abandonment of every ordinary skill. Learning, professional ability, careful observation, and compassionate attention can be placed within the mission of God. Luke’s enduring companionship would later become especially precious when others were absent.

Demas is named without either criticism or special commendation. At this point he stands among Paul’s associates and sends greetings to the Colossians. Later, however, Paul would write that Demas had forsaken him, “having loved this present world.” The later failure should not be read backward as though Paul were secretly condemning him here. Colossians records his genuine association with the mission at this moment.

Together the two names offer a sober lesson about perseverance. Present involvement, proximity to faithful leaders, and participation in gospel work do not make continued faithfulness automatic. Luke remained; Demas later departed. Christian endurance depends upon an ongoing attachment to Christ rather than yesterday’s service or present reputation. The brevity of the greeting therefore leaves both encouragement and warning: ordinary abilities can become instruments of devoted love, but every disciple must continue choosing the coming kingdom over the attractions of the present age.

verses.bibleText: Salute the brethren which are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the church which is in his house.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The circle of greeting now crosses from Paul’s place of confinement to the believers at Laodicea. Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis were neighboring communities, and their congregations maintained active fellowship. Paul wants the Colossians to see themselves as part of a wider body rather than as an isolated group facing its difficulties alone.

The KJV follows a textual tradition that reads “Nymphas” and “his house.” Other early witnesses support the feminine name “Nympha” and the reading “her house,” which many modern translations adopt. Because ancient Greek manuscripts were commonly written without the accents that would distinguish the masculine and feminine forms, and because the pronouns also vary, certainty is difficult. The safest conclusion is that Nymphas or Nympha was a Christian householder who opened a home for the congregation. The feminine reading may be somewhat more likely, but the verse does not provide enough information to define the person’s precise office.

Early Christian congregations commonly assembled in private homes. A household large enough to receive a group became a place for public reading of Scripture, prayer, instruction, fellowship, the breaking of bread, and care for those in need. Offering such a home required generosity and could expose the host to inconvenience, expense, and social risk. Hospitality therefore became a substantial ministry rather than a minor courtesy.

The wording also reminds the church that sacred identity is not created by a building. The house is a meeting place; the people called together in Christ are the church. Homes, occupations, possessions, and social influence can all be placed at the Lord’s service. Nymphas or Nympha is remembered because private resources were opened for communal blessing. The greeting honors both the host and the congregation, joining them to the larger fellowship of believers throughout the Lycus Valley.

wordNotes.term: the church which is in his house — τὴν κατ’ οἶκον ... ἐκκλησίαν (tēn kat’ oikon ... ekklēsian)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase describes a congregation gathering in a private household. The church is the assembled people, while the home provides the place in which they worship, learn, share fellowship, and organize their common life.

verses.bibleText:
And when this epistle is read among you, cause that it be read also in the church of the Laodiceans; and that ye likewise read the
epistle
 from Laodicea.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The command to exchange letters reveals how apostolic teaching was received within the earliest congregations. Colossians was not intended for a private individual or a small circle of advanced students. It was to be read aloud before the assembled church so that all could hear its teaching, warnings, prayers, and exhortations. Tychicus may have performed the reading and provided explanation where necessary.

Public reading gave the letter a corporate function. The congregation heard together that Christ is supreme over creation and the church, that salvation is complete in Him, and that new life must shape worship, speech, households, and relationships. The community could then encourage and correct one another in light of the same message. Scripture forms a people, not merely a collection of private religious opinions.

The Colossians must also arrange for their letter to be read in Laodicea. Its teaching addressed a particular situation, yet its truth possessed significance beyond the original recipients. Neighboring churches could learn from warnings and instructions first given elsewhere. This exchange also strengthened unity by placing both congregations under the same apostolic gospel.

“The epistle from Laodicea” most naturally means a letter that would come to Colossae from Laodicea, probably one previously addressed to the Laodicean believers. Its identity is unknown. Some have suggested Ephesians because of its probable circulation in Asia and its close relationship to Colossians, but the wording does not establish that conclusion. Later writings claiming to be the missing Laodicean letter have no sound claim to apostolic authority.

The absence of this particular letter need not imply that a necessary part of God’s saving revelation has been lost. Apostles wrote more communications than were preserved in the canonical collection, just as prophets and disciples performed more acts than Scripture records. God preserved the writings needed to bear authoritative witness to Christ and His will. The verse discourages speculation about what is unavailable and directs attention toward hearing, sharing, and obeying the inspired word that has been given.

wordNotes.explanation: The verb refers here to the letter being read aloud before the assembled congregation. Public reading enabled the whole church, including those unable to read or obtain a copy, to hear and respond to apostolic teaching.

verses.bibleText: And say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfil it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
A final charge is sent through the whole congregation to Archippus. He is mentioned elsewhere only in Philemon, where Paul calls him a “fellowsoldier.” His placement near Philemon, Apphia, and the church meeting in their house suggests that he held some recognized responsibility, but Scripture does not identify his family relationship, precise office, or assigned task. Claims that he was Philemon’s son, the pastor of Colossae, or a particular church officer remain possibilities rather than established facts.

The command “say to Archippus” is addressed to the congregation. His ministry is personal, but it is not private. The church has a responsibility to encourage, remind, and, where necessary, admonish those who serve it. This is not permission for faultfinding or public humiliation. Paul’s words recognize Archippus as one who has genuinely received a ministry while calling him to exercise it faithfully.

“Take heed” demands sustained attention. Ministry can be neglected through discouragement, distraction, fear, weariness, conflict, or misplaced ambition. Archippus must watch both the task and himself. Faithfulness requires more than beginning with enthusiasm; it requires continuing until the responsibility has been fulfilled.

The ministry was received “in the Lord.” Its origin and sphere are therefore decisive. Archippus has not created a platform for personal advancement, nor does he ultimately serve at the congregation’s pleasure. Christ has entrusted the service, Christ defines its character, and Christ supplies the grace needed to perform it. This also limits every claim to ministry: no calling from the Lord authorizes conduct contrary to the Lord’s word or character.

“Fulfil it” points toward completion rather than prominence. The value of ministry lies in obedience to the assignment given, whether or not that assignment appears impressive. The congregation must help Archippus remember this calling, while he must respond by carrying it through. Healthy Christian fellowship combines encouragement with accountability. Leaders need communities that neither flatter them nor continually discourage them, but lovingly call them to finish the work received from Christ.

wordNotes.explanation: The word denotes service or an entrusted task. It need not identify Archippus as holding the formal office of deacon; his particular responsibility may have involved teaching, pastoral care, administration, or another form of gospel service.

wordNotes.term: fulfil it — ἵνα αὐτὴν πληροῖς (hina autēn plērois)
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase calls Archippus to carry his service through to its intended completion. He must not leave unfinished what the Lord has entrusted to him.

verses.bibleText:
The salutation by the hand of me Paul. Remember my bonds. Grace
be with you. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The dictated letter ends in Paul’s own hand. Ancient letter writers commonly used a secretary, and Paul sometimes added a final greeting personally. His handwriting authenticates the message and gives the conclusion an unmistakably personal character. The church has not received an abstract theological essay but a pastoral appeal from a real servant suffering for the gospel.

“Remember my bonds” gathers several themes of the closing section into one brief command. Paul has already asked prayer for an open door through which the word may advance. His chains remind the Colossians that proclaiming Christ can involve real loss, shame, restriction, and pain. They are to remember him in prayer and fellowship, but the words reach beyond sympathy. His imprisonment demonstrates that suffering is not evidence that Christ has abandoned His servant or that the gospel has lost its power.

The command also places moral weight upon the letter. A prisoner for Christ has written to warn them against teachings that diminish Christ’s sufficiency. His bonds call them to value the gospel for which he suffers and to resist treating its truth casually. Yet Paul does not make his suffering the source of his authority or seek admiration for personal heroism. He remains a servant whose strength comes from the Lord.

The final word is “grace.” Colossians began with grace and peace and testified that the gospel had taught the believers the grace of God in truth. It now closes in the same atmosphere. The commands to pray, walk wisely, speak graciously, treat others justly, persevere in ministry, and stand mature are not a system for earning acceptance. They describe the life produced in people who have been reconciled through Christ and continue to depend upon Him.

Grace does not make obedience unnecessary; it makes faithful obedience possible and directs all glory to God. Paul is chained, the church is vulnerable, and its servants are imperfect, but divine grace remains with the whole congregation. Human circumstances cannot imprison it. The letter therefore ends neither with the chains nor with the danger of false teaching, but with the sustaining favor of God in Christ.

wordNotes.term: Remember my bonds — μνημονεύετέ μου τῶν δεσμῶν (mnēmoneuete mou tōn desmōn)
wordNotes.explanation: The command calls the congregation to keep Paul’s imprisonment actively in mind through prayer, solidarity, practical concern, and renewed courage in the gospel for which he suffers.

Grace is God’s freely given favor and saving action in Christ. Its position as the final word places every command, warning, ministry, and hope of the letter within divine generosity rather than human merit.
